headline: Australia: 697,000 used prescribed medicinal cannabis in 2025
dek: Penington Institute puts Australia's prescribed medicinal cannabis users at about 697,000 in 2025, 30 times 2019, with 60% getting scripts by telehealth.
key_points: About 697,000 Australians used prescribed medicinal cannabis in 2025, up from roughly 209,000 in 2022-23 and 23,400 in 2019, the Penington Institute estimated on 27 November from the national household drug survey.
Telehealth dominates access: 60% of people using only prescribed cannabis said it was their usual source of a script, against 25% who saw a doctor in person.
Non-prescribed use edged down to 10.6% of Australians aged 14 and over, from 11.5%, while edibles almost doubled as the main form among illicit users.
The growth sits awkwardly with regulators' 2025 crackdown on high-volume prescribing, and with a high-profile telehealth prescriber now cleared to return under supervision.
body: Australia's medicinal cannabis market has become one of the largest prescription programmes in the world by headcount. The Penington Institute, a Melbourne public-health organisation, estimated on 27 November that about 697,000 Australians used prescribed medicinal cannabis in 2025. That compares with around 209,000 in 2022-23 and just 23,400 in 2019, a near 30-fold rise in six years. The institute rounded the figure up to 'upwards of 700,000'.

The estimate is drawn from the latest National Drug Strategy Household Survey, the government's main population survey on drug use. It lands as Australian regulators are still working through a crackdown on high-volume telehealth prescribing that began in 2025, and the same data show that telehealth is now the main door into the system.

The headline is scale. Medicinal cannabis has been legal on prescription in Australia since 2016, for conditions where approved treatments have failed, but for most of that time it was a niche. The new estimate means prescribed use more than tripled between the last two surveys alone.

The source of supply has shifted just as sharply. Data released on 26 November by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW), as reported by The Marijuana Herald, put the number of Australians aged 14 and over who used cannabis for medical purposes in 2025 at about one million, or 4.3% of that age group, counting people who used it without a prescription. Among those medical users, 55% got their cannabis only through a doctor's prescription, up from 22% in 2022-23 and 1.8% in 2019. The share relying only on non-prescribed cannabis fell from 70% to 30% between the two latest surveys.
In other words, Australians who already used cannabis for health reasons have moved in large numbers from the illicit market into the legal, prescribed one.

Among people who used only doctor-prescribed medicinal cannabis, 60% said telehealth was their usual source of a prescription, compared with 25% who had an in-person consultation, according to Penington. That ratio explains both the growth and the regulatory backlash.

In July 2025 the national practitioner regulator, Ahpra, issued guidance targeting high-volume prescribing of medicinal cannabis, and Penington data published in April 2026 showed sales fell 28.5% in the second half of 2025 as the enforcement took effect, as recorded on MetaFlora's Australia legal hub. The new survey covers 2025 as a whole, so it captures the peak of telehealth-led growth before and during that squeeze.

The case of one prescriber shows where the line now sits. Cannabiz, an Australian trade outlet, reported this week that Dr Justin Welsh, who wrote about 2,000 medicinal cannabis scripts a month as a single-operator telehealth practitioner, has been cleared to prescribe again under strict supervision more than a year after the Medical Board of Australia barred him. The ban followed an Ahpra investigation into his prescribing volumes and SafeScript compliance issues, alongside concerns from WA Health about cross-state prescribing, Cannabiz said. The terms of his supervision were not public.
> Australia proved that a prescription channel can pull patients out of the illicit market. The fight now is over how fast doctors should be allowed to write those scripts.

Penington stressed that the boom in prescriptions has not been matched by a rise in recreational use. The share of Australians aged 14 and over reporting non-prescribed cannabis use in the past year fell slightly, from 11.5% in 2022-23 to 10.6% in 2025, while lifetime use edged up from 40.6% to 41.3%. The institute's chief executive, John Ryan, cautioned that illicit use is likely to be under-reported because people are reluctant to disclose it.

How people consume is changing. Among illicit users, edibles almost doubled as the main form of use, from 8.7% to 16.3%, while flower's share fell from 85.5% to 75.2%. Public opinion has cooled a little: according to the AIHW policy data cited by The Marijuana Herald, 41.1% of Australians support legalising cannabis for personal use and 37.5% oppose it, down from 44.6% support in 2022-23 but far above the 27% recorded in 2004.

For producers and importers, 697,000 patients is a large addressable base in a country that still bans adult-use sales nationwide; only the Australian Capital Territory allows adults to hold small amounts and grow two plants, and even there selling is an offence. But a big patient count does not guarantee healthy margins. As we reported on 15 November, Australian cultivators told StratCann that flower imported from Canada and Thailand now undercuts what many domestic growers can produce it for, pushing some to export or sell their sites.

The survey also hints at product demand. If edibles are rising fast among illicit users, prescribed formats beyond dried flower could become more important as regulators tighten scrutiny of high-volume flower scripts. That is an inference, not a finding of the survey.

Penington said its annual Cannabis in Australia 2026 report, due for release in mid-December, will set out use, access, supply and policy trends in more detail. Watch for prescription and sales data from 2026 to show whether the 2025 crackdown cut patient numbers or only the volume each patient receives. Watch also how Ahpra and medical boards treat other high-volume telehealth prescribers after Welsh's supervised return, and whether import pressure from Canada and Thailand forces more consolidation among Australian growers.
